explanation: “Mere presence” means simply being there: the girl is comforted just because the chair exists in the room with her, before anything else (like its rocking) is mentioned. Nothing in the text compares the chair with other furniture or says it goes unnoticed, so A and D add ideas the text doesn't support.

The text says marketing “gradually drew in customers” and that opinion later “had changed,” so diners must at first have pushed back against the chains. “Resisted” captures that early reluctance. “Discovered” or “prepared” don't set up the contrast with the later change in opinion.

The period is described as one of “flourishing literary production,” and the next sentence calls it a “flood of interesting writing,” so writers contributed to a large amount, or abundance, of work. “Erasure” and “underappreciation” suggest loss or neglect, the opposite of flourishing.

The second sentence uses “whereas” to show that active and quiet regions behave differently: one has energy drops after UV bursts, the other doesn't. A difference between two things is a disparity. “Analogy” would mean they are similar, and “trade-off” implies giving up one thing for another, which the text never describes.

After describing the two inventions, the underlined sentence names traits that both inventors had (creative thinking, problem-solving, persistence) and says these traits still drive innovation in general. That is a list of shared qualities that inventors rely on. Choice D is tempting, but the sentence describes the inventors, not features of their inventions.

fix.passage: In 1903, Mary Anderson patented a device that cleared rain and snow from a car’s windshield, improving visibility for drivers. In 1886, Josephine Cochrane invented a machine that washed dishes more efficiently, easing a time-consuming household task. Although designed to solve different problems, both inventions have had lasting effects. <u>Likewise, both inventors exemplified important traits that continue to drive innovation: creative thinking, strong problem-solving skills, and persistence.</u>

explanation: The underlined sentence begins with “However” and describes a surprising reaction from some shoppers: they see prices ending in 9 as signs of low quality or even as misleading. This implies the strategy doesn't always work. Choice D is tempting, but the usual reaction is described in the previous sentence, not the underlined one, and A wrongly says consumers “generally” react this way.

fix.passage: Sellers and advertisers often use prices ending in 9 (for example, $7.99) to make items seem like a better value. In many cases, shoppers respond as intended, viewing such prices as signs of a discount or special offer. <u>However, studies have found that some consumers connect these prices with lower-quality goods and even see them as misleading—an attempt to make a $7.99 item seem like it costs $7 rather than $8, which is closer to the truth.</u>

explanation: Lady Venom excuses Lord Arthur because he is witty, while Clara says wit combined with malice loses her respect. Fairman then says that even laughing at a cruel joke makes you part of the harm, which backs Clara and undercuts Lady Venom's excuse. He isn't explaining Lord Arthur's behavior (B), and he agrees with Clara rather than contrasting with her (C).

fix.passage:
The following text is from Frances Burney’s 1784 satirical play The Busy Salon. Clara, Lady Venom, and Edward Fairman are discussing their mutual acquaintance Lord Arthur Sharp.

CLARA: [Lord Arthur] has done nothing—but his talk is a perpetual slander on all his acquaintances.
FAIRMAN: Aye, and the worst of it is there is no advantage in not knowing him, for he’ll abuse a stranger just as soon as his closest friend—and [his cousin] is as bad.
LADY VENOM: Nay, but we should make allowance. Lord Arthur is a wit and a poet.
CLARA: For my part—I admit, madam—wit loses its respect with me when I see it in company with malice. What say you, Mr. Fairman?
FAIRMAN: <u>Certainly, madam, to smile at the jest that leaves a wound in another’s heart is to become a principal in the mischief.</u>

explanation: The text admits chickweed is seen as a nuisance but says weeds like it “can offer certain advantages,” such as reducing soil erosion. So the main point is that some weeds are useful. The other choices mention details (North America, gardening) without capturing that point.

The text defines division of labor, gives a backpack-factory example, and explains that workers become more skilled and save time, increasing production. All of this explains how the system improves efficiency. Zippers and backpacks are only part of the example, not the focus.

The Mole now sees the frightening wood “in a very different way”: the holes, traps, and other dangers are disappearing under a bright blanket of snow. So the snow makes the landscape seem safe instead of threatening. Nothing in the text mentions embarrassment, sadness, or a preference for warm weather.

The researchers say their model maximizes profit but may not suit firms that need to keep cash outflows (costs) low. The table supports this: the proposed model has the highest profit ($11,344,003) but also the highest total cost ($30,933,469), while the lexicographic model costs less and still beats the heuristic model's profit. Choice A is accurate but says nothing about costs, so it doesn't support the conclusion.

fix.passage: Because biofuels usually produce less carbon than fossil fuels, they can help reduce emissions. In California, biofuel producers have two sources of revenue: biofuel sales and LCFS (low carbon fuel standard) credits bought from them by companies whose fuel does not meet the state’s emissions standards. Considering how these revenue streams affect one another, Aylin Karaca et al. studied three models for how a biofuel company might maximize profit: the industry-standard heuristic model, a lexicographic model, and a model proposed by the researchers. They concluded that although their model maximized profit, it might not be the best option for firms that need to minimize cash outflows.

explanation: The claim is that Archer's social circle prefers the familiar to the new. Choice B shows that even though people talked of a grand new opera house, fashionable society was “still content” to return to the shabby old Academy each winter. Choice A is about Newland's own changed reactions, not the group's preference for the familiar.

The text notes that willingness to walk to transit depends on factors like well-enforced low speed limits. If enforcement in this neighborhood has increased a lot since the survey was taken ten years ago, residents' willingness to walk has probably changed, so the old survey would no longer reflect current views. Choice B is about rain in all of Portland and doesn't show any change over the ten years.

Flushing is dominated by Mandarin, a northern Chinese language, while Chinatown is dominated by Cantonese and Fuzhounese, southern languages. The logical inference is that immigrants from the north tend to settle in Flushing and those from the south in Chinatown. So the louder preference can't be explained by the musicians having damaged hearing. Choice D goes too far: the text never rules out musical expertise as a cause; it only rules out hearing loss.

The event happened in 1911 (“when it was introduced in 1911”), and the next sentence uses the past tense “wrote,” so the past-tense verb “faced” is needed. The present and future forms don't fit a completed past event.
The relative pronoun “which” refers to the singular noun “This invisible border,” so it needs the singular verb “is.” “Were,” “are,” and “have been” are plural forms.

The opening phrase “Originally introduced in 2017 and later optimized…” must describe the noun that comes right after the comma. The Retina Net algorithm is what was introduced and optimized, so “the Retina Net algorithm” must follow the comma. The other choices place “high accuracy” or “less computational power” there, creating a dangling modifier.

Both the part before the blank and the part after (“the handfish's modified pectoral fins function much like legs…”) are complete sentences, and the second explains the first. A colon correctly joins them and introduces the explanation. A comma alone creates a comma splice, no punctuation creates a run-on, and “and” without a comma doesn't properly join two long independent clauses here.

Several policy analysts have access, so the plural possessive “analysts’” is needed, and the data belong to many countries, so “countries’” is also plural possessive. Choice A uses singular forms, and C and D drop needed apostrophes.

The text follows the iguana through the day: at dawn it warms in the sun, and then, as the day gets hotter, it seeks shade. “Later” marks this step forward in time. “Previously” reverses the order, and “For example” doesn't fit because the second sentence isn't an example of the first.

explanation: The second sentence explains that negative pressure is useful: it pulls fresh air into the kitchen and helps contain cooking odors. So engineers balance airflow in order to produce, or create, those conditions. “Prevent” is the tempting trap, but it contradicts the benefits the text describes.

The electrician needs “this information” to figure out whether one device or too many devices caused the outage, so tenants must list the devices that were in use. “Itemize” means to list one by one. Activating, exchanging, or refurbishing devices wouldn't provide information.

Indirect stand-in measures are called proxies. “Simulations” are models, not things tracked in the field, and “parameters” doesn't convey the idea of an indirect indicator.

The chief's name “breathes valor and life / And courage to the people,” meaning it gives or inspires those qualities in his people. “Imparts” means gives or passes on. “Relinquishes” and “surrenders” suggest giving something up in defeat, and “absorbs” reverses the direction.

The underlined portion presents Feuer's view, as an expert, that film-studies concepts fell short for television. The next sentence says “Recognizing those limits, researchers turned to” new approaches, so her observation sets up the reason for the change in methods. Choice C overstates it as the “primary catalyst” for the whole field, which the text never claims.

fix.passage: Early television criticism in the 1970s and 1980s drew heavily on film studies, <u>though media scholar Jane Feuer observed that concepts borrowed from that discipline often fell short when applied to television’s distinctive features.</u> Recognizing those limits, researchers turned to approaches that considered home viewing environments, built-in commercials, and episodic storytelling, as well as to audience studies using ethnographic methods that highlighted viewer participation. By the 1990s, television studies had become a broadly established academic field, with scholars launching specialized journals.

Noting that regular samples had average concentrations of 0.90 mg/L of dissolved organic carbon (DOC) and 0.19 mg/L of total dissolved nitrogen (TDN) across events, the student concluded that contact with trees changes the chemical composition of rainwater before it reaches the ground.

explanation: Studying philosophy means knowing the field's foundational texts and figures; doing philosophy means creatively applying that acquired expertise and treating past thinkers as “vital interlocutors” (conversation partners) who help produce new insights. So doing philosophy builds on what is learned by studying it. Choice D is tempting, but the text never says doing philosophy requires challenging past ideas.

LCOE includes material-acquisition costs. If getting materials for new cells costs more than recycling old ones, then a shorter lifetime means cells are replaced more often, and the extra cost of new materials adds up faster, widening the cost gap. Choice A doesn't explain why operating costs would differ between the two kinds of plants.

fix.passage: After showing that the power-conversion efficiency of newly developed perovskite solar cells is nearly the same as that of cells recycled several times, Meilin Zhou and colleagues calculated the levelized cost of electricity (LCOE)—the cost per unit of electricity generated, including both material-acquisition and operating expenses—for power plants using each type of cell. Assuming a 15-year cell lifetime, the LCOE for plants using new cells was 4.99 cents per kilowatt-hour, whereas the LCOE for plants using cells recycled three times was 4.05 cents per kilowatt-hour. <u>Furthermore, when the assumed cell lifetime was reduced by two-thirds, the LCOE difference increased from 18.8% to 31.3%.</u>

explanation: The underlined claim is that the Dixie dingo supports the idea that precontact American dogs descend from Asian dogs, based on its Northeast Asian haplotype. If modern Northeast Asian breeds were brought to the Gulf Coast in the 1900s and may be among its recent ancestors, the haplotype could come from them rather than from ancient migration, undermining the claim. Choices A and D would, if anything, support the claim.

fix.passage: The Qimmig, an Arctic breed believed to date to before Europeans arrived in the Americas, descends from a precontact dog population. The Qimmig carries a haplotype (a group of genetic variants inherited together from one parent) absent in European dogs but present in Northeast Asian dogs, supporting the idea that precontact breeds in the Americas descend from dogs that accompanied human migration from Asia during the last ice age. <u>The Dixie dingo, a tan-coated breed native to the rural Gulf Coast of the United States, offers additional support</u>: living individuals carry haplotype B217, part of a haplotype group unique to Northeast Asian dogs. Many other precontact breeds, such as Canada’s Tahltan bear dog, disappeared through interbreeding with dogs brought from Europe.

That shift shows that ideas about authorship depend on the context in which works are written and published. The subject is the singular noun “courtly entertainment”; the phrase between the dashes is just an aside. It needs a singular past-tense verb, “was,” since the text describes a past era. “Were” and “are” are plural, and “being” doesn't give the sentence a main verb.

The sentence's main verb is “was disproved,” and its subject is “A 1932 report.” The blank begins a phrase that describes the report, so it needs a nonfinite form: “a report … asserting that …” A finite verb like “asserted” would give the subject two main verbs and make the sentence ungrammatical.

The first sentence says the sculpture is at Millennium Park, an outdoor space. “There” refers back to that location and explains why the sculpture faces rain, snow, and heat. “However” and “Nevertheless” signal a contrast that isn't present, and “In addition” doesn't capture the cause-and-place link.

Mintaka is very bright despite being 1,400 light-years away. Three resistors total 70 ohms, and the other five are positive but at most 40 each, adding more than 0 and at most 5 × 40 = 200. So x is greater than 70 and at most 70 + 200 = 270: 70 < x ≤ 270. Choice B forgets to add the 70.

(1/6)^x is always positive and can get as close to 0 as you like, so (1/6)^x + 8 is always greater than 8 and f(x) = 7((1/6)^x + 8) is always greater than 56, getting arbitrarily close to 56. So the greatest k with f(x) > k for all x is 56. Choice B forgets to multiply by 7.

explanation: Move everything to one side: (x − a)(x − 31) − (x − a) = 0, then factor out (x − a): (x − a)(x − 31 − 1) = (x − a)(x − 32) = 0. The solutions are x = a and x = 32. Plugging in 31 gives 31 − a = 0, which is false since a > 32.

explanation: f(a) = 4a − 6, so f(a) + 1 = 4a − 5. Set it equal to 3a: 4a − 5 = 3a, which gives a = 5.
Increasing by 150% means multiplying by 1 + 1.50 = 2.50 each period. The period is 19 days, so the exponent is x/19: y = 8(2.50)^(x/19). Choice B uses 1.50, which would be only a 50% increase.

77.8°F is the largest value, so removing it lowers the mean: I must be true. For the median, the original 11 values have their 6th value in the 50–55 bin; the new median is the average of the 5th and 6th values, which are also both in the 50–55 bin. If those two values are equal, the median doesn't change, so II doesn't have to be true.

fix.prompt:
The maximum temperature on April 1, in degrees Fahrenheit (°F), was recorded each year at a certain weather station for 11 years. The histogram summarizes the recorded data set.

The temperature of 77.8°F is removed from this data set to create a new data set of 10 temperatures. Which of the following statements must be true?
I. The mean of the new data set is less than the mean of the original data set.
II. The median of the new data set is less than the median of the original data set.

explanation: a = 23.14(b + c) and b = 0.89c, so c = b/0.89. Then a = 23.14(b + b/0.89) = 23.14 · (1.89/0.89) · b ≈ 49.14b. So a is about 4,914% of b. Choice B, 49.14%, forgets to convert the multiplier 49.14 into a percent.
One cubic yard is 3 × 3 × 3 = 27 cubic feet. So 145,800 cubic feet equals 145,800/27 = 5,400 cubic yards. Dividing by 3 instead of 27 is the common mistake; the depth of 12 feet isn't needed.

The base area is 16, so each base side is 4. The four triangular faces have total area 8sqrt(965), so each has area 2sqrt(965) = (1/2)(4)(l), giving slant height l = sqrt(965). The height, half the base side (2), and the slant height form a right triangle: h^2 = 965 − 2^2 = 961, so h = 31.

fix.prompt: A right square pyramid has a surface area of 16 + 8sqrt(965) square inches, which includes a base area of 16 square inches. What is the height, in inches, of this pyramid?

explanation: WX is the altitude to the hypotenuse, so angle WXY equals angle Z (both are 90° minus angle Y). In right triangle XWY, tan(∠WXY) = WY/WX = 588/441 = 4/3. Therefore tan Z = 4/3. Choice B, 3/4, is tan Y.

explanation: In vertex form, y = −a(x − 1)^2 + 19 = −ax^2 + 2ax + (19 − a). So b = 2a and c = 19 − a. Since c must be a positive integer, a ≤ 18, so the greatest b is 2 · 18 = 36.
